reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with a subjective feeling of unsteadiness on standing still that is promptly relieved by sitting, walking or leaning on support
The tremor is a high-frequency oscillation (characteristically about 13 to 18 Hz) of the legs and trunk that is often not visible but may be palpable or audible on auscultation over the leg muscles
Patients describe a fear of falling when standing still, although actual falls are relatively uncommon early on
The high frequency is highly specific and is best confirmed with surface electromyography
Symptoms are absent when the legs are unloaded and appear within seconds of standing
It most often affects older adults and is more common in women
It is under-recognised and frequently misattributed to anxiety or a non-specific balance disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Primary orthostatic tremor is characterised by a highly synchronous, high-frequency oscillation affecting the weight-bearing leg and trunk muscles, thought to originate from a central generator that may involve the brainstem and cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits. The tremor appears only when the legs are loaded during standing and resolves once that load is removed, producing the characteristic relief on sitting or walking. Its remarkable frequency and its high coherence between different muscles distinguish it from other tremors.
additionalDifferentials: Parkinson's disease and other parkinsonian syndromes
Cerebellar ataxia and other gait disorders
additionalInvestigations: Surface electromyography of the leg muscles demonstrating the characteristic high-frequency, highly coherent tremor, which is the key diagnostic investigation
Clinical assessment comparing symptoms on standing with those on sitting and walking
MRI brain where a secondary or structural cause is suspected
DAT imaging where coexisting parkinsonism is suspected (orthostatic-tremor-plus)
Assessment for peripheral neuropathy and vestibular dysfunction
Review of medication and metabolic contributors to unsteadiness
redFlags: Rapidly progressive unsteadiness or frequent falls suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Associated parkinsonism, ataxia or focal signs indicating a secondary cause
Onset in a young patient, which is atypical
reference.prognosis: Primary orthostatic tremor is usually slowly progressive and, although it can be disabling because of the persistent fear of falling and limited standing tolerance, it is not life-shortening. Response to pharmacotherapy is often partial and may wane over time, and selected refractory patients have been treated with deep brain stimulation. Practical measures such as using a stool or walking to relieve symptoms help maintain function.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because the tremor is not visible; palpation, auscultation and surface EMG are needed
Misattributing symptoms to anxiety or a primary balance disorder
Failing to distinguish primary orthostatic tremor from orthostatic-tremor-plus syndromes with parkinsonism
Overlooking the characteristic relief on sitting or walking within the history
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Consensus statement on the classification of tremors (Movement Disorders)
management: Clonazepam as the usual first-line drug, with gabapentin a common alternative or add-on for this often only partially responsive tremor
Trial of further agents such as primidone, valproate, levetiracetam or a dopaminergic agent where response is inadequate
Occupational adaptations to minimise prolonged standing — a perching stool, a walking aid and opportunities to sit or walk — since symptoms remit on unloading the legs
Physiotherapy and falls-prevention strategies addressing the disabling fear of falling while standing still
Reassessment for emerging parkinsonism (orthostatic-tremor-plus), with dopaminergic treatment where a synucleinopathy is confirmed
Referral to a movement-disorder neurologist and consideration of thalamic deep brain stimulation in selected, severely refractory patients
